title: CLUSTERS OF PRIMES REVISITED

paper.title: CLUSTERS OF PRIMES REVISITED
paper.abstract: Abstract We revisit the generalized Rayleigh quotient optimization problem related to the Maynard-Tao sieve with the goal of finding a more efficient function basis. We demonstrate that a family based on products of reciprocals, previously used in asymptotic estimates for H m = lim inf n → ∞ ( p n + m − p n ) H_{m}=\liminf_{n\rightarrow\infty}(p_{n+m}-p_{n}) , provides results that are close to the theoretical limits of the sieve across many regimes. In particular, we obtain: H 2 ≤ 31 140 , H 3 ≤ 2 560 022 , H 4 ≤ 193 672 056 , H 5 ≤ 13 659 045 840 . H_{2}\leq 31\,140,\quad H_{3}\leq 2\,560\,022,\quad H_{4}\leq 193\,672\,056,\quad H_{5}\leq 13\,659\,045\,840. We also show that, as k → ∞ k\to\infty , the related variational quantity M k M_{k} , introduced by Maynard [ 6 ] , satisfies the lower bound M k ≥ log ⁡ k − 0.273572 + o ⁡ ( 1 ) . M_{k}\geq\log k-0.273572+o(1).

sections.heading: 1 Introduction
sections.text: In this paper, we study upper bounds for H m := lim inf n → ∞ ( p n + m − p n ) H_{m}:=\liminf_{n\to\infty}(p_{n+m}-p_{n}) . The first unconditional finite bound of this kind was established by Zhang [ 16 ] , who proved that H 1 ≤ 70 000 000 H_{1}\leq 70\,000\,000 . Soon afterward, Maynard [ 6 ] developed a different approach and obtained H 1 ≤ 600 H_{1}\leq 600 and H m ≪ m 3 ​ exp ⁡ ( 4 ​ m ) H_{m}\ll m^{3}\exp(4m) . Both of these breakthroughs led to successive phases of the Polymath8 project, which aimed to push the newly developed techniques to their limits [ 8 , 9 ] . The bounds H 1 ≤ 246 H_{1}\leq 246 , H 2 ≤ 398 130 H_{2}\leq 398\,130 , H 3 ≤ 24 797 814 H_{3}\leq 24\,797\,814 (and similar for larger m m ) were established and remained untouched for many years. Eventually, Julia Stadlmann obtained slightly stronger bounds for H m H_{m} for m = 2 , 3 , 4 , 5 m=2,3,4,5 as a corollary of her result concerning primes in arithmetic progressions [ 13 ] : H 2 ≤ 396 504 , H 3 ≤ 24 407 016 , H 4 ≤ 1 391 051 532 , H 5 ≤ 77 510 685 234 . H_{2}\leq 396\,504,\quad H_{3}\leq 24\,407\,016,\quad H_{4}\leq 1\,391\,051\,532,\quad H_{5}\leq 77\,510\,685\,234. Recently, she also established H 1 ≤ 240 H_{1}\leq 240 by finding a way to combine ideas from Maynard’s and Zhang’s approaches [ 14 ] . A concurrent preprint by Hanxin Zhang [ 15 ] reported the same bound. Several further preprints claim improvements to the bound for H 1 H_{1} using various strategies [ 5 , 12 , 2 , 7 ] . Recent Progress . This paper was developed independently of the recent preprint by Roeling [ 10 ] , of which the author became aware only when this project was already at an advanced stage. The methods used are different, and the results obtained here are slightly stronger. Very recently, another preprint [ 4 ] reports further improvements to the numerical bounds on H m H_{m} for m = 2 , 3 , 4 , 5 m=2,3,4,5 by incorporating enlarged sieve support and the methods developed in [ 7 ] . The resulting bounds are stronger than those presented here, in particular H 2 ≤ 20 370 H_{2}\leq 20\,370 . Concerning the asymptotic results, Theorem 3 remains unmatched in the current literature, as far as the author is aware. The starting point in all modern approaches to the problem of short gaps between primes is the GPY setup [ 3 ] with some variant of the Selberg sieve, usually the Maynard–Tao sieve. We begin with an expression of the form 𝒮 ⁡ ( x , k , m , ℋ , Λ Sel 2 ) = ∑ x < n ≤ 2 ​ x ( ∑ h ∈ ℋ 𝟏 𝐏 ​ ( n + h ) − m ) ​ Λ Sel 2 ​ ( n , ℋ ) , \mathcal{S}(x;k,m,\mathcal{H},\Lambda^{2}_{\mathrm{Sel}})=\sum_{x<n\leq 2x}\left(\sum_{h\in\mathcal{H}}\mathbf{1}_{\mathbf{P}}(n+h)-m\right)\,\Lambda^{2}_{\mathrm{Sel}}(n;\mathcal{H}), (1) where ℋ \mathcal{H} is an admissible k k -tuple and Λ Sel 2 \Lambda^{2}_{\mathrm{Sel}} are appropriately chosen non-negative weights that are designed to detect good candidates for primes. If we can demonstrate that there exist arbitrarily large values of x x such that 𝒮 > 0 , \mathcal{S}>0, then an upper bound for H m H_{m} follows. Of course, ideally Λ Sel 2 \Lambda^{2}_{\mathrm{Sel}} would detect primes exclusively, but even for k = 2 k=2 this would require arithmetic information well beyond our reach (the parity barrier). In practice, the best we can hope for with currently known sieve techniques is to retain a sufficiently high density of primes among the remaining candidates. This can lead to non-trivial bounds on H m H_{m} .

sections.text: We now introduce the necessary terminology and briefly describe how the Maynard-Tao sieve transforms prime detection into an optimization problem. sections.heading: Sources of improvements
sections.text: To summarize the discussion, we can describe the usual framework as follows: GPY set-up ⟶ dealing with the error term ⟶ optimization problem . \text{GPY set-up}\quad\longrightarrow\quad\text{dealing with the error term}\quad\longrightarrow\quad\text{optimization problem}. Historically, since the set-up itself was used for the first time, researchers have been finding improvements in all of the links of the above chain: 1. We can expand the sieve support by deploying stronger distributional claims than the Bombieri-Vinogradov theorem. This is the strategy Zhang followed to get the first result showing that H 1 H_{1} is indeed finite [ 16 ] . The key innovations of Stadlmann may also belong to this category [ 13 , 14 ] . 2. Instead of focusing on BV-type claims, we can expand the sieve support by using various arithmetic tricks. One example of this sort is the ε \varepsilon -trick, first described in [ 9 ] . 3. One can instead modify the GPY framework itself. A prominent example is Maynard’s key idea of considering multidimensional Selberg weights. Another approach of this kind is to replace the prime indicator function 𝟏 𝐏 \mathbf{1}_{\mathbf{P}} with a suitable minorant [ 1 ] . 4. We can focus on the resulting optimization problems. In [ 9 ] , a substantial effort was put into numerical calculations involving M k M_{k} and M k , ε M_{k,\varepsilon} to obtain H 1 ≤ 246 H_{1}\leq 246 unconditionally and H 1 ≤ 6 H_{1}\leq 6 assuming the generalized Elliott-Halberstam conjecture. Another example in this category is searching for shorter admissible k k -tuples. While this part is already optimized in the most interesting m = 1 m=1 case, there is still some room for improvement for m ≥ 2 m\geq 2 . The approach of this paper sits firmly in the fourth category: the key motivation for this project was to study the variational quotient M k M_{k} (as well as M k , ε M_{k,\varepsilon} ) for middle-sized k ≈ 50 k\approx 50 , where some interesting novelties concerning H 1 H_{1} may possibly lie. The key presumption was that these quotients can be estimated in a more efficient way than using high-degree symmetric polynomials, as in [ 9 , 14 ] . In this project, several families of functions were tested. Even when k k is very large, we evaluate the key integrals I ε ​ ( F ) I_{\varepsilon}(F) and J ε ​ ( F ) J_{\varepsilon}(F) directly. We demonstrate that a family based on products of reciprocals, previously used in asymptotic estimates for H m = lim inf n → ∞ ( p n + m − p n ) H_{m}=\liminf_{n\rightarrow\infty}(p_{n+m}-p_{n}) , provides results that are close to the theoretical limits of the sieve across many regimes. In particular, we obtain: H 2 ≤ 31 140 , H 3 ≤ 2 560 022 , H 4 ≤ 193 672 056 , H 5 ≤ 13 659 045 840 . H_{2}\leq 31\,140,\quad H_{3}\leq 2\,560\,022,\quad H_{4}\leq 193\,672\,056,\quad H_{5}\leq 13\,659\,045\,840. We also show that, as k → ∞ k\to\infty , the related variational quantity M k M_{k} , introduced by Maynard [ 6 ] , satisfies the lower bound M k ≥ log ⁡ k − 0.273572 + o ⁡ ( 1 ) . M_{k}\geq\log k-0.273572+o(1). 1 Introduction In this paper, we study upper bounds for H m := lim inf n → ∞ ( p n + m − p n ) H_{m}:=\liminf_{n\to\infty}(p_{n+m}-p_{n}) . The first unconditional finite bound of this kind was established by Zhang [ 16 ] , who proved that H 1 ≤ 70 000 000 H_{1}\leq 70\,000\,000 . Soon afterward, Maynard [ 6 ] developed a different approach and obtained H 1 ≤ 600 H_{1}\leq 600 and H m ≪ m 3 ​ exp ⁡ ( 4 ​ m ) H_{m}\ll m^{3}\exp(4m) . Both of these breakthroughs led to successive phases of the Polymath8 project, which aimed to push the newly developed techniques to their limits [ 8 , 9 ] . The bounds H 1 ≤ 246 H_{1}\leq 246 , H 2 ≤ 398 130 H_{2}\leq 398\,130 , H 3 ≤ 24 797 814 H_{3}\leq 24\,797\,814 (and similar for larger m m ) were established and remained untouched for many years. Eventually, Julia Stadlmann obtained slightly stronger bounds for H m H_{m} for m = 2 , 3 , 4 , 5 m=2,3,4,5 as a corollary of her result concerning primes in arithmetic progressions [ 13 ] : H 2 ≤ 396 504 , H 3 ≤ 24 407 016 , H 4 ≤ 1 391 051 532 , H 5 ≤ 77 510 685 234 . H_{2}\leq 396\,504,\quad H_{3}\leq 24\,407\,016,\quad H_{4}\leq 1\,391\,051\,532,\quad H_{5}\leq 77\,510\,685\,234. Recently, she also established H 1 ≤ 240 H_{1}\leq 240 by finding a way to combine ideas from Maynard’s and Zhang’s approaches [ 14 ] . A concurrent preprint by Hanxin Zhang [ 15 ] reported the same bound. Several further preprints claim improvements to the bound for H 1 H_{1} using various strategies [ 5 , 12 , 2 , 7 ] . Recent Progress . This paper was developed independently of the recent preprint by Roeling [ 10 ] , of which the author became aware only when this project was already at an advanced stage. The methods used are different, and the results obtained here are slightly stronger. Very recently, another preprint [ 4 ] reports further improvements to the numerical bounds on H m H_{m} for m = 2 , 3 , 4 , 5 m=2,3,4,5 by incorporating enlarged sieve support and the methods developed in [ 7 ] . The resulting bounds are stronger than those presented here, in particular H 2 ≤ 20 370 H_{2}\leq 20\,370 . Concerning the asymptotic results, Theorem 3 remains unmatched in the current literature, as far as the author is aware. The starting point in all modern approaches to the problem of short gaps between primes is the GPY setup [ 3 ] with some variant of the Selberg sieve, usually the Maynard–Tao sieve. We begin with an expression of the form 𝒮 ⁡ ( x , k , m , ℋ , Λ Sel 2 ) = ∑ x < n ≤ 2 ​ x ( ∑ h ∈ ℋ 𝟏 𝐏 ​ ( n + h ) − m ) ​ Λ Sel 2 ​ ( n , ℋ ) , \mathcal{S}(x;k,m,\mathcal{H},\Lambda^{2}_{\mathrm{Sel}})=\sum_{x<n\leq 2x}\left(\sum_{h\in\mathcal{H}}\mathbf{1}_{\mathbf{P}}(n+h)-m\right)\,\Lambda^{2}_{\mathrm{Sel}}(n;\mathcal{H}), (1) where ℋ \mathcal{H} is an admissible k k -tuple and Λ Sel 2 \Lambda^{2}_{\mathrm{Sel}} are appropriately chosen non-negative weights that are designed to detect good candidates for primes. If we can demonstrate that there exist arbitrarily large values of x x such that 𝒮 > 0 , \mathcal{S}>0, then an upper bound for H m H_{m} follows. Of course, ideally Λ Sel 2 \Lambda^{2}_{\mathrm{Sel}} would detect primes exclusively, but even for k = 2 k=2 this would require arithmetic information well beyond our reach (the parity barrier). In practice, the best we can hope for with currently known sieve techniques is to retain a sufficiently high density of primes among the remaining candidates. This can lead to non-trivial bounds on H m H_{m} . From primes to functional optimization We now introduce the necessary terminology and briefly describe how the Maynard-Tao sieve transforms prime detection into an optimization problem. Starting from an expression of the form ( 1 ), we expand the Selberg weights, swap the sums, and obtain something of the form: 𝒮 = MT 𝟏 𝐏 − m ⋅ MT 1 + ( BV-type error ) , \mathcal{S}=\mathrm{MT_{\mathbf{1}_{\mathbf{P}}}}-m\cdot\mathrm{MT_{1}}+(\text{BV-type error}), (2) where the main terms give rise to certain integral functionals to be optimized later. The error term is closely related to the distributional claims concerning primes in arithmetic progressions of the Bombieri-Vinogradov type. Better results in this area lead to larger sieve supports. Recall some key notation and concepts. We closely follow the notation introduced by Polymath8b. Definition 1 (Standard simplex) . For any θ > 0 \theta>0 and any integer k ≥ 1 k\geq 1 , we define the rescaled standard simplex as the set θ ⋅ ℛ k := { ( t 1 , … , t k ) ∈ [ 0 , + ∞ ) k : t 1 + ⋯ + t k ≤ θ } . \theta\cdot\mathcal{R}_{k}:=\left\{(t_{1},\ldots,t_{k})\in[0,+\infty)^{k}\colon t_{1}+\cdots+t_{k}\leq\theta\right\}.
